name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
presentation: A middle-aged woman wakes at night with numb, painful hands that she shakes to relieve, and drops small objects during the day. Tingling involves the thumb, index and middle fingers and the radial half of the ring finger but spares the little finger and the palm; the thenar eminence is wasted in advanced cases and thumb abduction is weak. Tapping the wrist (Tinel) or holding it flexed (Phalen) reproduces the tingling.

deficits.distribution: palmar thumb, index, middle and radial ring finger
deficits.sign: Nocturnal paresthesias and later sensory loss in the median digital distribution, sparing the thenar palm
Thenar wasting and weak thumb abduction and opposition; long flexors spared

reasoning: The median nerve enters the hand beneath the flexor retinaculum in the carpal tunnel together with the nine flexor tendons, and any increase in the contents or decrease in the space of the tunnel compresses it: tenosynovitis, fluid retention in pregnancy, hypothyroidism, acromegaly, amyloid, diabetes and repetitive wrist flexion. Compression damages the large myelinated fibers first, producing paresthesias that are worst at night when the wrist flexes during sleep and venous congestion rises. The palmar cutaneous branch leaves the nerve above the tunnel and passes over the retinaculum, so sensation over the thenar eminence is spared, a point that separates carpal tunnel syndrome from a proximal median lesion or a C6–C7 radiculopathy. The motor branch to the thenar muscles arises within or just beyond the tunnel, so the abductor pollicis brevis and opponens waste while the flexor pollicis longus and the pronator, supplied in the forearm, are normal; the first two lumbricals are also affected but are hard to test. The lesion is peripheral and ipsilateral, and though it is often bilateral, one hand usually dominates. Nerve conduction shows slowing across the wrist with normal forearm conduction, which confirms the site. Sensory symptoms that include the little finger, the forearm, or weakness of the finger flexors point elsewhere.

imagingFindings.finding: Prolonged median distal sensory and motor latencies across the wrist with normal ulnar values; denervation of the abductor pollicis brevis in severe cases.
Enlarged cross-sectional area of the median nerve proximal to the tunnel (above about 10 mm²) with flattening beneath the retinaculum.
Ganglion, tenosynovitis, amyloid or anomalous muscle within the carpal tunnel in atypical cases.

commonCauses: Pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, acromegaly, rheumatoid arthritis

mimics.name: C6–C7 radiculopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Neck pain, sensory loss including the forearm and thenar palm, reflex change, normal distal latencies

mimics.name: Pronator syndrome (proximal median)
mimics.howToDistinguish: Thenar palm numb, forearm pain, flexor pollicis longus weak

mimics.name: Polyneuropathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Bilateral, symmetric, feet involved, sural response abnormal

mimics.name: Thoracic outlet syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Medial forearm sensory loss and interosseous weakness

management: Night splints and activity modification; treat the underlying condition
Corticosteroid injection into the tunnel for temporary relief
Surgical release for persistent symptoms, sensory loss or thenar wasting
